paragraphs.text: Dear elders and sisters, hopefully each of you have been blessed by the ordinance of the sacrament today and have been able to renew your devotion to God and your purpose as a full-time missionary. This is an important time to do it on the Sabbath. It'll fortify you for the whole week ahead. I want to discuss a very important topic with you, but let me first share a story.

There was once a family with three small children. The children were very determined to have a puppy. Now, their mom protested because she knew that somehow or other she would end up taking care of the dog. However, the children begged and promised and committed that they would take care of the dog if they would just be able to have one. Eventually the mother gave in and the family went out and bought a little puppy and brought it home.

The children named him Danny and cared for him diligently at first, but sure enough, as time passed, mom found herself becoming more and more responsible for taking care of the dog. Finally she decided that the children were not living up to their promise, so she began to search for a new home for Danny. When she found one and broke the news to the children, she was quite surprised that they had almost no reaction at all. One of them even said, "Well, I guess we'll miss him." "I'm sure we will," mom answered, "but he has just too much work for one person, and since I'm the one who has to do all the work, I say he needs to go." "But," protested another child, "if you wouldn't eat so much and wouldn't be so messy, could we keep him?" Mom held her ground. It's time to take Danny to his new home. Suddenly, with one voice and with tears in their eyes, the children exclaimed, "Danny? We thought you said Daddy!"

That's a funny story, but it's going to make a point that I hope we never see among your children when you have a family. Because next Sunday is Father's Day. I want to share some thoughts with you about fathers. That funny story, as I said, sadly sometimes is quite true for children in our world, yet it shouldn't be. It should never be true for the children to be one day yours that they're not that sad about losing their daddy. Let me share a few thoughts that I've gathered and experienced that might help you when you come to those days. Sisters, while this podcast seems focused on the elders, I assure you that it is very important to you. You need to be very wise in your selection of who the father is going to be of your children. So pay attention to this as well.

Now each of us have a father here on earth. Maybe your father was wonderful in every way and you are so grateful for him. Maybe your father wasn't such a good example and you don't feel a very strong bond to him or even any bond at all. Well, we must always remember that we each also have another father, our Father in Heaven. He is a perfect example in every way. Each of you elders will become a father and each of you sisters will marry the father to your children. Because of the great importance of fathers, I want to define father in a way that you can remember and maybe have impact in how you choose to be a father. When I learned this from another good man, it helped me. I wish I'd have learned it earlier. But we can take each letter in the word father and tie it to another word to help us remember what a good father should be and what you elders should expect to be for your children when the time comes that you have a family.

The word father begins with F, which you can remember as faith. You cannot be the best father possible unless you have a deep and personal faith in God. Regardless of how much you love your children and regardless of what you do to care for them, if you've never come to know your Father in Heaven through the Savior Jesus Christ, you will fall very short of God's expectation for you as a father. The reason: your children need a father who knows the Father. And if you ever expect your children to know their Father in Heaven and have faith in him, you must first possess and demonstrate that faith in your Heavenly Father.

Many years ago, a farmer and his family, after a hard year of typical farm work, were rewarded with an unusually fine crop of grain. They were very happy about this and they expected happy days ahead. Unfortunately, just a few days before the harvest, there came a terrible wind and hail storm. The entire crop was destroyed. After the storm was over, the farmer with his wife and little son at his side went out to the back porch to view the field and the damage. It was completely devastated. The little boy looked at what was formerly a beautiful field of grain and tearfully looked up at his dad, expecting to hear words of despair. All at once, his father started to sing softly: "Rock of Ages, cleft for me, let me hide myself in thee." Years later, the little boy, now a growing man, said, "That was the greatest sermon I've ever heard." The farmer had lost a grain crop, but because of his faith manifested in this great trial, he had deeply impressed on the soul of his son how we should all trust God. The son never forgot the faith of his father.

The next letter in father is A. We will use adversity to remember this letter in father. What should be our response when adversity comes our way? How should we handle it? When the storms of life beat upon us and we struggle for answers, what should we do? Psalm 86, verse 7 says: "In the day of my trouble I will call upon thee: for thou wilt answer me." Turning to our Father in Heaven in our adversity is the exact right first step. We should not turn to him only in times of trouble, but when we are in times of trouble and adversity, prayer to him should be our first action and our children should see that example.

Next, Psalm 119, verse 138 says: "Thy testimonies that thou hast commanded are righteous and very faithful." After our prayers, we should turn to the words of God in the scriptures and the teachings of the modern prophets. You have heard it said that when you want to talk with God, you pray, and when you want God to talk to you, it is best to read the scriptures. This is a great second step in your season of adversity.

In Psalm 5, verse 7, King David said: "But as for me, I will come into thy house in the multitude of thy mercy: and in thy fear will I worship toward thy holy temple." This is a great third step—getting to church and to the temple where we can meditate in the spirit and receive personal revelation to help us get through our adversity. Fathers should remember that their children are always watching.

A large family once sat around the table for breakfast. As was the tradition in the family, the father prayed, giving thanks to God for the food. But immediately afterward, he began to grumble about the poor quality of the food and much more that he didn't like that day. One of his little girls spoke up, "Daddy, do you suppose God heard what you prayed a little while ago?" "Why, certainly," the father replied with confidence. And the little girl said, "And did he remember what you said about the food after you prayed? About it not being very good?" The father replied with a little less confidence, "I think so." Then his little girl asked him, "Then Daddy, which of those statements did God believe?"

Children will always remember how a dad took the family through the trials of life. Did he whine or shine? As fathers, we will all leave behind a legacy. The one most remembered will be the one remembered by our children. Fathers need to set the right example now so that when they are gone, the children will know exactly how to face adversity in their lives. They will be able to say, "This is the way my dad did it, and that's what we're going to do. We will trust God." In the Bible, God commanded the fathers to teach their children and to set an example so that according to Psalm 78, verse 7: "That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments."

The next letter in Father is T. We will use teacher as a way to remember this important aspect of a father's role. Carl Jung, the great psychiatrist, said: "Children are educated by what the grown-up is and not by his talk." A father's example is far more important than his words. And for a father to set a great example, he has to be available. Yes, we all know that fathers have to work. And yes, we understand that there are many other duties that are required of a father's time, but there's nothing more important than the time you invest in teaching your children. Make certain they are in their church meetings. Make certain there is time for prayers and devotions at home. Make certain that you're available to help with schoolwork. Be available.

Recently, I read this story and it had a big impact on me. I wish I had read it sooner when my children were younger. It's a true story and maybe, hearing it now, it will help you be better than I was as a father in this regard. The man started with this story. He said: "When I was just 12 and my Boy Scout troop planned a father-and-son campout, I was thrilled and could hardly wait to rush home and give my father all the information. I wanted so much to show him all that I had learned in scouting and I was so proud when he said he would go with me. The Friday of the campout finally came and I had all my gear out on the porch ready to stuff it into his car the moment he arrived. We were supposed to meet at the local school at 5 p.m. and carpool to the campground, but dad didn't get home from work until 7 p.m. He explained how things had gone wrong at work and told me not to worry—we could still get up first thing in the morning and join the others. After all, we had a map. I was disappointed, of course, but decided to just make the best of it."

The man continued: "First thing in the morning, I was up early and had everything in his car while it was still getting light, all ready for us to catch up with my friends and their fathers at the campground. He had said we'd leave around 7 and I was ready a half an hour before that, but he never came out of his room until 9. When he saw me standing out in front with the camping gear, he finally explained that he had a bad back and he couldn't sleep on the ground. He hoped I'd understand and I'd be a big boy about it, but could I please get my things out of the car because he had several commitments he had to keep. Just about the hardest thing I've ever done was to go to the car and take out my sleeping bag, cooking stove, my little tent and supplies. And then, while I was putting my stuff away in the storage shed and he thought I couldn't see, I watched my father carry his golf clubs out and throw them in the trunk of the car and drive away to keep his commitment. That's when I realized my dad never meant to go with me to the campout. I didn't matter to him, but his golfing buddies did."

This father taught his son a lesson. He taught him that he could not be trusted to keep his word. This boy never forgot that lesson. In fact, as a grown man, he later wrote this story and shared it before a gathering of men and fathers in a leadership conference. We need to never forget that in order for us to teach our children—whether it has to do with church or schoolwork or family devotions or anything, even lessons in camping—we have to be available and we have to be honorable.

The next letter in Father is H. H stands for helper. A good father is a helper. He's a helper to his wife and he's a helper to his children. A smart father knows that helping his wife with all her many duties is the best way to create a great relationship with his wife and a great example to his children. A father who does the dishes and helps clean the house will have a grateful wife and children who grow up with the right idea about building healthy relationships in their family. A father who helps with the homework, he helps with school projects, he helps attend the children's activities, and he's a listening ear when a child needs to talk—he takes time to be involved. He's always there with an arm to lean on. Ken Canfield, in his book The Seven Secrets of Effective Fathers, said: "Effective fathers are committed to their children, know their children, are consistent in their attitudes and behavior, protect and provide for their children, love their children's mother, are active listeners to their children, spiritually equip their children." So then, a father is a helper. He's a helper to his wife and he's a helper to his children.

The next letter in Father is E. E stands for encouragement. One of the best ways to encourage our children is by letting them know we care. We care when they fall down and get hurt. We care when they've had a bad day at school. We care when their friends have hurt their feelings. We care when their special plans didn't turn out the way they'd hoped. A father should be one of the best friends his children have. Another way to encourage children is by showing them that we can forgive. Sometimes parents, especially fathers, can be too hard on their children. Certainly there is a time for discipline and for instruction, but there is also a time to show forgiveness. I'm glad our Heavenly Father forgives us, aren't you? When children do wrong things—and they will—once we have corrected the problem, we need to sit down and put our arm around them and say, "What you did was wrong, but I forgive you and I love you." That will go a long way with your children. They will never forget it. Encourage your children by forgiving them.

The final letter in Father is R. R stands for reputation. I was very grateful my father had a good reputation. He was a man who did the right thing and he did his work well. He was very unhealthy with many health challenges and was in the hospital for much of my growing up years, but he still managed to provide for our family. We didn't have much, but we had enough to live. He often told me that while he couldn't leave me with any money or land as an inheritance, he was going to leave me with the most valuable thing he had and the most valuable thing anyone could have, which was a good name, and he did. And I will always be grateful for the effort and discipline he made and gave to make sure all his children inherited a good name and reputation.

Elders, remember, your reputation is important. It's important to your children. It's important to God, and it ought to be very important to you. And you're building that reputation right now, one day at a time, one decision at a time. Proverbs 22, verse 1 says: "A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold." I can testify that this verse of scripture is so very true. Building a great reputation and name are not easy, however, and you won't get one by taking the easy way out. Remember this poem when you are tempted to take the easy road: "The easy roads are crowded and the level roads are jammed. The pleasant little rivers with the drifting folk are crammed. But off yonder where it's rocky, where you get a better view, you will find the ranks are thinning and the travelers are few."

How do you spell Father? Faith, adversity, teacher, helper, encouragement, reputation. In conclusion, let me share a prayer written by General Douglas MacArthur when he was here in the Philippines during the early and very desperate days of World War II. He wrote this prayer for his son: "Build me a son, O Lord, who will be strong enough to know when he is weak, and brave enough to face himself when he is afraid; one who will be proud and unbending in honest defeat, and humble and gentle in victory. Build me a son whose wishes will not take the place of deeds; a son who will know Thee—and that to know himself is the foundation stone of knowledge. Lead him, I pray, not in the path of ease and comfort, but under the stress and spur of difficulties and challenge. Here let him learn to stand up to the storm; here let him learn compassion for those who fail. Build me a son whose heart will be clear, whose goal will be high; a son who will master himself before he seeks to master other men; who will reach into the future, yet never forget the past. And after all these things are his, add, I pray, enough of a sense of humor, so that he may always be serious, but never take himself too seriously. Give him humility, so that he may always remember the simplicity of true greatness, and an open mind of true wisdom, and the meekness of true strength. Then I, his father, will dare to whisper, 'I have not lived in vain.'"

So elders, I pray that God will give you the strength and courage to live now in a way that you will be the example you want your children to follow. Sisters, I pray that when the time comes for you to choose a father for your children, you will focus on the faith and the character of the man and not on anything else. Those two attributes will allow you to make the best choice in a husband and a father for your future children. Good night elders and sisters. We love you.
